There is, indeed, no sublimity in him so far as he is subject to the moral law. But inasmuch as, in regard to that very law, he is likewise a legislator, and on that account alone subject to it, he has sublimity. We have also shown above that neither fear nor inclination, but simply respect for the law, is the spring that can give actions a moral worth. Our own will, so far as we suppose it to act only under the condition that its maxims are potentially universal laws — this ideal will, which is possible to us — is the proper object of respect; and the dignity of humanity consists precisely in this capacity of being universally legislative, though with the condition that it is itself subject to this same legislation.

3.94.oldText: Autonomy of the will is that property of it by which it is a law to itself (independently of any property of the objects of volition). The principle of autonomy, then, is: "Always so to choose that the same volition shall comprehend the maxims of our choice as a universal law." We cannot prove that this practical rule is an imperative — that is, that the will of every rational being is necessarily bound to it as a condition — by a mere analysis of the conceptions occurring in it, since it is a synthetical proposition. We must advance beyond the cognition of the objects to a critical examination of the subject — that is, of pure practical reason — for this synthetical proposition, which commands apodeictically, must be capable of being cognized wholly a priori. This matter, however, does not belong to the present section. But that the principle of autonomy in question is the sole principle of morals can be readily shown by mere analysis of the conceptions of morality. For by this analysis we find that its principle must be a categorical imperative, and that what this commands is neither more nor less than this very autonomy.

3.97.oldText: If the will seeks the law that is to determine it anywhere else than in the fitness of its maxims to be universal laws of its own dictation — if, consequently, it goes outside itself and seeks this law in the character of any of its objects — heteronomy always results. The will in that case does not give itself the law; the law is given to it by the object through its relation to the will. This relation, whether it rests on inclination or on conceptions of reason, only admits of hypothetical imperatives: "I ought to do something because I wish for something else." On the contrary, the moral, and therefore categorical, imperative says: "I ought to do so and so, even though I should not wish for anything else." For example, the former says: "I ought not to lie if I wish to retain my reputation"; the latter says: "I ought not to lie, even if it should not bring me the least discredit." The latter therefore must abstract entirely from all objects, so that they shall have no influence on the will — in order that practical reason (will) may not be restricted to administering an interest not belonging to it, but may simply show its own commanding authority as the supreme legislation. For example, I ought to endeavour to promote the happiness of others, not as if its realization involved any concern of mine (whether by immediate inclination or by any satisfaction indirectly gained through reason), but simply because a maxim that excludes it cannot be comprehended as a universal law in one and the same volition.

3.100.oldText: Here, as elsewhere, human reason in its pure use, so long as it was not critically examined, has first tried all possible wrong ways before it succeeded in finding the one true way.

3.101.oldText: All principles that can be taken from this point of view are either empirical or rational. The former, drawn from the principle of happiness, are built on physical or moral feelings. The latter, drawn from the principle of perfection, are built either on the rational conception of perfection as a possible effect, or on that of an independent perfection (the will of God) as the determining cause of our will.

3.102.oldText: Empirical principles are wholly incapable of serving as a foundation for moral laws. For the universality with which moral laws should hold for all rational beings without distinction, the unconditional practical necessity thereby imposed on them, is lost when their foundation is taken from the particular constitution of human nature or the accidental circumstances in which it is placed. The principle of private happiness, however, is the most objectionable — not merely because it is false, and experience contradicts the supposition that prosperity is always proportioned to good conduct; nor yet merely because it contributes nothing to the establishment of morality (since it is quite a different thing to make a prosperous man and a good man, or to make a person prudent and sharp-sighted for his own interests and to make him virtuous); but because the springs it provides for morality are such as rather undermine it and destroy its sublimity, since they put the motives to virtue and to vice in the same class and only teach us to make a better calculation, the specific difference between virtue and vice being entirely extinguished. On the other hand, as to moral feeling, this supposed special sense * — the appeal to it is indeed superficial when those who cannot think believe that feeling will help them out even in what concerns general laws. Besides, feelings, which naturally differ infinitely in degree, cannot furnish a uniform standard of good and evil, nor does anyone have a right to form judgements for others by his own feelings. Nevertheless this moral feeling is nearer to morality and its dignity in this respect: that it pays virtue the honour of ascribing to her immediately the satisfaction and esteem we have for her, and does not, as it were, tell her to her face that we are not attached to her by her beauty but by profit.

3.103.oldText: * I class the principle of moral feeling under that of happiness, because every empirical interest promises to contribute to our well-being by the agreeableness that a thing affords, whether immediately and without a view to profit, or whether profit is regarded. We must likewise, with Hutcheson, class the principle of sympathy with the happiness of others under his assumed moral sense.

3.104.oldText: Among the rational principles of morality, the ontological conception of perfection, despite its defects, is better than the theological conception that derives morality from a Divine absolutely perfect will. The former is no doubt empty and indefinite, and consequently useless for finding in the boundless field of possible reality the greatest amount suitable for us. Moreover, in attempting to distinguish specifically the reality of which we are now speaking from every other, it inevitably tends to turn in a circle, and cannot avoid tacitly presupposing the morality which it is to explain. It is nevertheless preferable to the theological view: first, because we have no intuition of the divine perfection and can only deduce it from our own conceptions, the most important of which is that of morality, so our explanation would thus be involved in a gross circle; and second, if we avoid this, the only notion of the Divine will remaining to us is a conception made up of the attributes of desire of glory and dominion, combined with the awful conceptions of might and vengeance — and any system of morals erected on this foundation would be directly opposed to morality.

3.105.oldText: However, if I had to choose between the notion of the moral sense and that of perfection in general (two systems that at least do not weaken morality, although they are totally incapable of serving as its foundation), I should decide for the latter, because it at least withdraws the decision of the question from the sensibility and brings it to the court of pure reason; and although even here it decides nothing, it at all events preserves the indefinite idea (of a will good in itself) free from corruption, until it shall be more precisely defined.

3.106.oldText: For the rest, I think I may be excused here from a detailed refutation of all these doctrines. That would only be superfluous labour, since the refutation is so easy, and is probably so well seen even by those whose office requires them to decide for one of these theories (because their hearers would not tolerate suspension of judgement). But what interests us more here is to know that the prime foundation of morality laid down by all these principles is nothing but heteronomy of the will, and for this reason they must necessarily miss their aim.

3.107.oldText: In every case where an object of the will has to be supposed in order that the rule may be prescribed that is to determine the will, there the rule is simply heteronomy; the imperative is conditional, namely: if, or because, one wishes for this object, one should act in such-and-such a way. Hence it can never command morally — that is, categorically. Whether the object determines the will by means of inclination, as in the principle of private happiness, or by means of reason directed to objects of our possible volition in general, as in the principle of perfection, in either case the will never determines itself immediately by the conception of the action, but only by the influence that the foreseen effect of the action has on the will. "I ought to do something, for this reason, because I wish for something else." And here yet another law must be assumed in me as its subject, by which I necessarily will this other thing; and this law again requires an imperative to restrict this maxim. For the influence that the conception of an object within the reach of our faculties can exercise on the will of the subject, in consequence of its natural properties, depends on the nature of the subject — either the sensibility (inclination and taste), or the understanding and reason, the employment of which is, by the peculiar constitution of their nature, attended with satisfaction. It follows that the law would, properly speaking, be given by nature; and, as such, it must be known and proved by experience, would consequently be contingent, and therefore incapable of being an apodeictic practical rule, such as the moral rule must be. Not only that, but it is inevitably only heteronomy: the will does not give itself the law, but is given the law by a foreign impulse, by means of a particular natural constitution of the subject adapted to receive it. An absolutely good will, then — whose principle must be a categorical imperative — will be indeterminate as regards all objects, and will contain merely the form of volition in general, namely as autonomy. That is to say, the capability of the maxims of every good will to make themselves a universal law is itself the only law that the will of every rational being imposes on itself, without needing to assume any spring or interest as a foundation.

3.108.oldText: How such a synthetical practical a priori proposition is possible, and why it is necessary, is a problem whose solution does not lie within the bounds of the metaphysics of morals. And we have not here affirmed its truth, much less professed to have a proof of it in our power. We simply showed, by the development of the universally received notion of morality, that an autonomy of the will is inevitably connected with it — or rather is its foundation. Whoever, then, holds morality to be anything real, and not a chimerical idea without any truth, must likewise admit the principle of it that is here assigned. This section, then, like the first, was merely analytical. To prove that morality is no creation of the brain — which it cannot be if the categorical imperative, and with it the autonomy of the will, is true and absolutely necessary as an a priori principle — supposes the possibility of a synthetic use of pure practical reason; which, however, we cannot venture on without first giving a critical examination of this faculty of reason. In the concluding section we shall give the principal outlines of this critical examination, as far as is sufficient for our purpose.

4.0.oldText: The Concept of Freedom is the Key that explains the Autonomy of the Will

4.1.oldText: The will is a kind of causality belonging to living beings so far as they are rational; and freedom would be that property of such causality by which it can be efficient independently of foreign causes determining it — just as physical necessity is the property that the causality of all irrational beings has of being determined to activity by the influence of foreign causes.

4.2.oldText: The preceding definition of freedom is negative and therefore unfruitful for the discovery of its essence; but it leads to a positive conception that is so much the more full and fruitful.

4.3.oldText: Since the conception of causality involves that of laws — according to which, by something we call cause, something else (namely the effect) must be produced — although freedom is not a property of the will depending on physical laws, it is not for that reason lawless. On the contrary, it must be a causality acting according to immutable laws, but of a peculiar kind; otherwise a free will would be an absurdity. Physical necessity is a heteronomy of efficient causes, since every effect is possible only according to this law: that something else determines the efficient cause to exert its causality. What else, then, can freedom of the will be but autonomy — that is, the property of the will to be a law to itself? But the proposition "The will is in every action a law to itself" only expresses the principle: "To act on no other maxim than one which can also have itself as an object as a universal law." Now this is precisely the formula of the categorical imperative, and is the principle of morality. So a free will and a will subject to moral laws are one and the same.

4.4.oldText: On the hypothesis, then, of freedom of the will, morality together with its principle follows from it by mere analysis of the conception. However, the latter is a synthetic proposition: an absolutely good will is one whose maxim can always include itself regarded as a universal law. For this property of its maxim can never be discovered by analysing the conception of an absolutely good will. Now such synthetic propositions are only possible in this way: that the two cognitions are connected together by their union with a third in which both are to be found. The positive concept of freedom furnishes this third cognition, which cannot, as with physical causes, be the nature of the sensible world (in the concept of which we find the concept of something in relation as cause to something else as effect). We cannot yet at once show what this third is to which freedom points us and of which we have an idea a priori; nor can we make intelligible how the concept of freedom is shown to be legitimate from principles of pure practical reason, and with it the possibility of a categorical imperative. Some further preparation is required.

4.5.oldText: Freedom must be presupposed as a Property of the Will

4.7.oldText: It is not enough to predicate freedom of our own will, on whatever ground, if we have no sufficient grounds for predicating the same of all rational beings. For since morality serves as a law for us only because we are rational beings, it must also hold for all rational beings; and since it must be deduced simply from the property of freedom, it must be shown that freedom too is a property of all rational beings. It is not enough, then, to prove it from certain supposed experiences of human nature (which is indeed quite impossible, and it can only be shown a priori); we must show that it belongs to the activity of all rational beings endowed with a will. Now I say: every being that cannot act except under the idea of freedom is, just for that reason, in a practical point of view really free. That is to say, all laws inseparably connected with freedom have the same force for him as if his will had been shown to be free in itself by a theoretically conclusive proof. * Now I affirm that we must attribute to every rational being that has a will the idea of freedom too, and that such a being acts entirely under this idea. For in such a being we conceive a reason that is practical — that is, has causality with reference to its objects. Now we cannot possibly conceive a reason as consciously receiving a bias from any other quarter with respect to its judgements; for then the subject would ascribe the determination of its judgement not to its own reason, but to an impulse. Reason must regard itself as the author of its principles, independent of foreign influences. Consequently, as practical reason, or as the will of a rational being, it must regard itself as free. That is to say, the will of such a being cannot be a will of its own except under the idea of freedom. This idea must therefore in a practical point of view be ascribed to every rational being.

4.8.oldText: * I adopt this method of assuming freedom merely as an idea that rational beings suppose in their actions, in order to avoid the necessity of proving it in its theoretical aspect as well. The former is sufficient for my purpose; for even if the speculative proof should not be made out, a being that cannot act except with the idea of freedom is bound by the same laws that would oblige a being who was actually free. We can thus escape here from the onus that presses on the theory.

4.9.oldText: Of the Interest attaching to the Ideas of Morality

4.10.oldText: We have finally reduced the definite conception of morality to the idea of freedom. The latter, however, we could not prove to be actually a property of ourselves or of human nature; we only saw that it must be presupposed if we would conceive a being as rational and conscious of its causality with respect to its actions — that is, as endowed with a will. And so we find that on just the same grounds we must ascribe to every being endowed with reason and will this attribute of determining itself to action under the idea of its freedom.

4.11.oldText: Now it also resulted from the presupposition of these ideas that we became aware of a law: that the subjective principles of action — that is, maxims — must always be so assumed that they can also hold as objective, that is, universal principles, and so serve as universal laws of our own dictation. But why, then, should I subject myself to this principle, and that simply as a rational being, thus subjecting to it all other beings endowed with reason too? I will allow that no interest urges me to this, for that would not give a categorical imperative; but I must take an interest in it and discern how this comes about. For this "I ought" is properly an "I would" valid for every rational being, provided only that reason determined his actions without any hindrance. But for beings that are additionally affected, as we are, by springs of a different kind — namely, sensibility — and in whose case what reason alone would do is not always done, that necessity is expressed only as an "ought," and the subjective necessity is different from the objective.

4.12.oldText: It seems, then, as if the moral law — that is, the principle of autonomy of the will — were properly speaking only presupposed in the idea of freedom, and as if we could not prove its reality and objective necessity independently. In that case we should still have gained something considerable by at least determining the true principle more exactly than had previously been done; but as regards its validity and the practical necessity of subjecting oneself to it, we should not have advanced a step. For if we were asked why the universal validity of our maxim as a law must be the condition restricting our actions, and on what we ground the worth we assign to this manner of acting — a worth so great that there cannot be any higher interest — and if we were asked further how it happens that it is by this alone that a human being believes he feels his own personal worth, in comparison with which that of an agreeable or disagreeable condition is to be regarded as nothing, to these questions we could give no satisfactory answer.

4.13.oldText: We do indeed sometimes find that we can take an interest in a personal quality that does not involve any interest of external condition, provided this quality makes us capable of participating in that condition in case reason were to effect the allotment — that is, the mere being worthy of happiness can interest us of itself, even without the motive of participating in this happiness. This judgement, however, is in fact only the effect of the importance of the moral law that we presupposed before (when by the idea of freedom we detached ourselves from every empirical interest). But that we ought to detach ourselves from these interests — that is, consider ourselves as free in action and yet as subject to certain laws, so as to find a worth simply in our own person which can compensate us for the loss of everything that gives worth to our condition — this we are not yet able to discern in this way. Nor do we see how it is possible so to act — in other words, from where the moral law derives its obligation.

4.14.oldText: It must be freely admitted that there is a sort of circle here from which it seems impossible to escape. In the order of efficient causes we assume ourselves free, in order that in the order of ends we may conceive ourselves as subject to moral laws; and we afterwards conceive ourselves as subject to these laws because we have attributed to ourselves freedom of will. For freedom and self-legislation of the will are both autonomy, and therefore are reciprocal conceptions; for this very reason one cannot be used to explain the other or to give the reason for it, but at most only to reduce, for logical purposes, apparently different notions of the same object to one single concept (as we reduce different fractions of the same value to the lowest terms).

4.15.oldText: One resource remains to us, namely, to inquire whether we do not occupy different points of view when by means of freedom we think of ourselves as causes efficient a priori, and when we form our conception of ourselves from our actions as effects we see before our eyes.

4.16.oldText: It is a remark that needs no subtle reflection to make, but which we may assume that even the commonest understanding can make (although it does so after its fashion by an obscure discernment of judgement which it calls feeling), that all the "ideas" that come to us involuntarily (as those of the senses) do not enable us to know objects otherwise than as they affect us; so that what they may be in themselves remains unknown to us. Consequently, as regards "ideas" of this kind, even with the closest attention and clarity the understanding can apply to them, we can attain through them only knowledge of appearances, never of things in themselves. As soon as this distinction has once been made — perhaps merely as a consequence of the difference observed between the ideas given us from without, in which we are passive, and those we produce simply from ourselves, in which we show our own activity — it follows of itself that we must admit and assume behind the appearance something else that is not an appearance, namely, the things in themselves; although we must admit that since these can never be known to us except as they affect us, we can come no nearer to them, nor can we ever know what they are in themselves. This must furnish a distinction, however crude, between a world of sense and a world of understanding; the former may differ according to the variation of sensuous impressions in various observers, while the second, which is its basis, always remains the same. Even as to himself, a human being cannot pretend to know what he is in himself from the knowledge he has by internal sensation. For since he does not, as it were, create himself, and does not come by the conception of himself a priori but empirically, it naturally follows that he can obtain his knowledge even of himself only through the inner sense, and consequently only through the appearances of his nature and the way in which his consciousness is affected. At the same time, beyond these characteristics of his own subject, made up of mere appearances, he must necessarily suppose something else as their basis, namely, his ego, whatever its characteristics in itself may be. Thus, in respect to mere perception and the receptivity of sensations, he must reckon himself as belonging to the world of sense; but in respect of whatever there may be of pure activity in him (what reaches consciousness immediately, and not through affecting the senses), he must reckon himself as belonging to the intellectual world — of which, however, he has no further knowledge. To such a conclusion the reflecting person must come with respect to all the things that can be presented to him. It is probably to be met with even in persons of the commonest understanding, who, as is well known, are very much inclined to suppose behind the objects of the senses something else invisible, acting of itself. But they spoil it by presently sensualizing this invisible again — that is, by wanting to make it an object of intuition — so they do not become a whit the wiser.

4.17.oldText: Now a human being really finds in himself a faculty by which he distinguishes himself from everything else, even from himself as affected by objects — and that is reason. This faculty, being pure spontaneity, is even elevated above the understanding. For although the latter is a spontaneity and does not, like sense, merely contain intuitions that arise when we are affected by things (and are therefore passive), it cannot produce from its activity any other conceptions than those that merely serve to bring the intuitions of sense under rules, and thereby unite them in one consciousness; and without this use of the sensibility it could not think at all. Whereas, on the contrary, reason shows so pure a spontaneity in the case of what I call ideas (ideal conceptions) that it thereby far transcends everything the sensibility can give it, and exhibits its most important function in distinguishing the world of sense from that of understanding, and thereby prescribing the limits of the understanding itself.

4.18.oldText: For this reason a rational being must regard himself qua intelligence (not from the side of his lower faculties) as belonging not to the world of sense but to that of understanding. Hence he has two points of view from which he can regard himself and recognize laws of the exercise of his faculties, and consequently of all his actions: first, so far as he belongs to the world of sense, he finds himself subject to laws of nature (heteronomy); secondly, as belonging to the intelligible world, under laws which, being independent of nature, have their foundation not in experience but in reason alone.

4.19.oldText: As a rational being, and consequently belonging to the intelligible world, a human being can never conceive the causality of his own will otherwise than on condition of the idea of freedom; for independence of the determinate causes of the sensible world (an independence which reason must always ascribe to itself) is freedom. Now the idea of freedom is inseparably connected with the conception of autonomy, and this again with the universal principle of morality, which is ideally the foundation of all actions of rational beings, just as the law of nature is of all phenomena.

4.20.oldText: Now the suspicion is removed that we raised above — that there was a latent circle involved in our reasoning from freedom to autonomy, and from this to the moral law — namely, that we laid down the idea of freedom on account of the moral law only that we might afterwards in turn infer the latter from freedom; and that consequently we could assign no reason at all for this law, but could only present it as a petitio principii that well-disposed minds would gladly concede to us, but which we could never put forward as a provable proposition. For now we see that when we conceive ourselves as free, we transfer ourselves into the world of understanding as members of it, and recognize the autonomy of the will with its consequence, morality; whereas if we conceive ourselves as under obligation, we consider ourselves as belonging to the world of sense and at the same time to the world of understanding.

4.21.oldText: How is a Categorical Imperative Possible?

4.22.oldText: Every rational being reckons himself qua intelligence as belonging to the world of understanding, and it is simply as an efficient cause belonging to that world that he calls his causality a will. On the other side, he is also conscious of himself as a part of the world of sense, in which his actions, which are mere appearances (phenomena) of that causality, are displayed. We cannot, however, discern how these actions are possible from this causality, which we do not know; instead of that, these actions as belonging to the sensible world must be viewed as determined by other phenomena, namely, desires and inclinations. If, therefore, I were only a member of the world of understanding, all my actions would perfectly conform to the principle of autonomy of the pure will; if I were only a part of the world of sense, they would necessarily be assumed to conform wholly to the natural law of desires and inclinations — in other words, to the heteronomy of nature. (The former would rest on morality as the supreme principle, the latter on happiness.) Since, however, the world of understanding contains the foundation of the world of sense, and consequently of its laws too, and accordingly gives the law to my will (which belongs wholly to the world of understanding) directly, and must be conceived as doing so, it follows that, although on the one side I must regard myself as a being belonging to the world of sense, on the other I must recognize myself as subject as an intelligence to the law of the world of understanding — that is, to reason, which contains this law in the idea of freedom — and therefore as subject to the autonomy of the will. Consequently I must regard the laws of the world of understanding as imperatives for me, and the actions that conform to them as duties.

4.23.oldText: And thus what makes categorical imperatives possible is this: that the idea of freedom makes me a member of an intelligible world, in consequence of which, if I were nothing else, all my actions would always conform to the autonomy of the will. But since I at the same time intuit myself as a member of the world of sense, they ought so to conform; and this categorical "ought" implies a synthetic a priori proposition. For besides my will as affected by sensible desires, there is added further the idea of the same will but as belonging to the world of understanding, pure and practical of itself, which contains the supreme condition according to reason of the former will — precisely as concepts of the understanding, which of themselves signify nothing but regular form in general, are added to the intuitions of sense; and in this way synthetic a priori propositions become possible, on which all knowledge of physical nature rests.

4.24.oldText: The practical use of common human reason confirms this reasoning. There is no one, not even the most consummate villain — provided only that he is otherwise accustomed to the use of reason — who, when we set before him examples of honesty of purpose, of steadfastness in following good maxims, of sympathy and general benevolence (even combined with great sacrifices of advantages and comfort), does not wish that he too might possess these qualities. Only on account of his inclinations and impulses he cannot attain this in himself; yet at the same time he wishes to be free from such inclinations, which are burdensome even to himself. He proves by this that he transfers himself in thought — with a will free from the impulses of the sensibility — into an order of things wholly different from that of his desires in the field of the sensibility. Since he cannot expect to obtain by that wish any gratification of his desires, nor any position that would satisfy any of his actual or supposable inclinations (for this would destroy the pre-eminence of the very idea that wrests that wish from him), he can only expect a greater intrinsic worth of his own person. This better person, however, he imagines himself to be when he transfers himself to the point of view of a member of the world of understanding — to which he is involuntarily forced by the idea of freedom, that is, of independence from determining causes of the world of sense. From this point of view he is conscious of a good will, which by his own confession constitutes the law for the bad will he possesses as a member of the world of sense — a law whose authority he recognizes while transgressing it. What he morally "ought" is then what he necessarily "would" as a member of the world of understanding, and is conceived by him as an "ought" only inasmuch as he likewise considers himself as a member of the world of sense.

4.25.oldText: Of the Extreme Limits of all Practical Philosophy.

4.26.oldText: All human beings attribute to themselves freedom of will. Hence come all judgements upon actions as being such as ought to have been done, although they have not been done. However, this freedom is not a conception of experience, nor can it be, since it still remains even though experience shows the contrary of what, on the supposition of freedom, are conceived as its necessary consequences. On the other side, it is equally necessary that everything that takes place should be fixedly determined according to laws of nature. This necessity of nature is likewise not an empirical conception, just for this reason, that it involves the notion of necessity and consequently of a priori cognition. But this conception of a system of nature is confirmed by experience; and it must even inevitably be presupposed if experience itself is to be possible — that is, a connected knowledge of the objects of sense resting on general laws. Therefore freedom is only an idea of reason, and its objective reality in itself is doubtful; while nature is a concept of the understanding which proves, and must necessarily prove, its reality in examples of experience.

4.27.oldText: From this there arises a dialectic of reason, since the freedom attributed to the will appears to contradict the necessity of nature; and, placed between these two ways, reason for speculative purposes finds the road of physical necessity much more beaten and more appropriate than that of freedom. Yet for practical purposes the narrow footpath of freedom is the only one on which it is possible to make use of reason in our conduct. Hence it is just as impossible for the subtlest philosophy as for the commonest reason of human beings to argue away freedom. Philosophy must then assume that no real contradiction will be found between freedom and physical necessity of the same human actions, for it cannot give up the conception of nature any more than that of freedom.

4.28.oldText: Nevertheless, even if we should never be able to comprehend how freedom is possible, we must at least remove this apparent contradiction in a convincing manner. For if the thought of freedom contradicts either itself or nature, which is equally necessary, it must, in competition with physical necessity, be entirely given up.

4.29.oldText: It would, however, be impossible to escape this contradiction if the thinking subject, which seems to itself free, conceived itself in the same sense or in the very same relation when it calls itself free as when, with respect to the same action, it assumes itself to be subject to the law of nature. Hence it is an indispensable problem of speculative philosophy to show that its illusion respecting the contradiction rests on this: that we think of the human being in a different sense and relation when we call him free and when we regard him as subject to the laws of nature as being part and parcel of nature. It must therefore show that not only can both these very well coexist, but that both must be thought as necessarily united in the same subject; since otherwise no reason could be given why we should burden reason with an idea which, although it may possibly without contradiction be reconciled with another that is sufficiently established, yet entangles us in a perplexity that sorely embarrasses reason in its theoretical employment. This duty, however, belongs only to speculative philosophy. The philosopher then has no option whether he will remove the apparent contradiction or leave it untouched; for in the latter case the theory respecting this would be bonum vacans, into the possession of which the fatalist would have a right to enter and chase all morality out of its supposed domain as occupying it without title.

4.30.oldText: We cannot, however, as yet say that we are touching the bounds of practical philosophy. For the settlement of that controversy does not belong to it; it only demands of speculative reason that it should put an end to the discord in which it entangles itself in theoretical questions, so that practical reason may have rest and security from external attacks which might make the ground debatable on which it desires to build.

4.31.oldText: The claims to freedom of will made even by common reason are founded on the consciousness, and the admitted supposition, that reason is independent of merely subjectively determined causes that together constitute what belongs to sensation only, and which consequently come under the general designation of sensibility. A human being who considers himself in this way as an intelligence places himself thereby in a different order of things, and in a relation to determining grounds of a wholly different kind, when on the one hand he thinks of himself as an intelligence endowed with a will (and consequently with causality), and when on the other he perceives himself as a phenomenon in the world of sense (as he really is also), and affirms that his causality is subject to external determination according to laws of nature. Now he soon becomes aware that both can hold good — indeed, must hold good at the same time. For there is not the smallest contradiction in saying that a thing in appearance (belonging to the world of sense) is subject to certain laws of which the very same thing, as a thing or being in itself, is independent. That he must conceive and think of himself in this twofold way rests, as to the first, on the consciousness of himself as an object affected through the senses, and as to the second, on the consciousness of himself as an intelligence — that is, as independent of sensible impressions in the employment of his reason (in other words, as belonging to the world of understanding).

4.32.oldText: Hence it comes to pass that a human being claims the possession of a will that takes no account of anything that comes under the head of desires and inclinations, and on the contrary conceives actions as possible for him — indeed, even as necessary — that can only be done by disregarding all desires and sensible inclinations. The causality of such actions lies in him as an intelligence, and in the laws of effects and actions that depend on the principles of an intelligible world — of which indeed he knows nothing more than that in it pure reason alone, independent of sensibility, gives the law. Moreover, since it is only in that world, as an intelligence, that he is his proper self (being as a human being only the appearance of himself), those laws apply to him directly and categorically, so that the incitements of inclinations and appetites (in other words, the whole nature of the world of sense) cannot impair the laws of his volition as an intelligence. Indeed, he does not even hold himself responsible for the former or ascribe them to his proper self — that is, his will. He only ascribes to his will any indulgence he might yield to them if he allowed them to influence his maxims to the prejudice of the rational laws of the will.

4.33.oldText: When practical reason thinks itself into a world of understanding, it does not thereby transcend its own limits, as it would if it tried to enter that world by intuition or sensation. The former is only a negative thought with respect to the world of sense, which does not give any laws to reason in determining the will, and is positive only in this single point: that this freedom as a negative characteristic is at the same time conjoined with a (positive) faculty, and even with a causality of reason, which we designate a will — namely, a faculty of so acting that the principle of the actions shall conform to the essential character of a rational motive, that is, the condition that the maxim have universal validity as a law. But if it were to borrow an object of the will — that is, a motive — from the world of understanding, it would overstep its bounds and pretend to be acquainted with something of which it knows nothing. The conception of a world of understanding is then only a point of view that reason finds itself compelled to take outside the appearances in order to conceive itself as practical; which would not be possible if the influences of the sensibility had a determining power on a human being, but which is necessary unless he is to be denied the consciousness of himself as an intelligence, and consequently as a rational cause, energizing by reason — that is, operating freely. This thought certainly involves the idea of an order and a system of laws different from that of the mechanism of nature, which belongs to the sensible world; and it makes the conception of an intelligible world necessary (that is to say, the whole system of rational beings as things in themselves). But it does not in the least authorize us to think of it further than as to its formal condition only — that is, the universality of the maxims of the will as laws, and consequently the autonomy of the will, which alone is consistent with its freedom; whereas, on the contrary, all laws that refer to a definite object give heteronomy, which only belongs to laws of nature and can only apply to the sensible world.

4.34.oldText: But reason would overstep all its bounds if it undertook to explain how pure reason can be practical, which would be exactly the same problem as explaining how freedom is possible.

4.35.oldText: For we can explain nothing but what we can reduce to laws whose object can be given in some possible experience. But freedom is a mere idea, the objective reality of which can in no way be shown according to laws of nature, and consequently not in any possible experience. For this reason it can never be comprehended or understood, because we cannot support it by any sort of example or analogy. It holds good only as a necessary hypothesis of reason in a being that believes itself conscious of a will — that is, of a faculty distinct from mere desire (namely, a faculty of determining itself to action as an intelligence, in other words, by laws of reason independent of natural instincts). Now where determination according to laws of nature ceases, all explanation ceases too, and nothing remains but defence — that is, the removal of the objections of those who pretend to have seen deeper into the nature of things and thereupon boldly declare freedom impossible. We can only point out to them that the supposed contradiction they have discovered in it arises only from this: that in order to be able to apply the law of nature to human actions, they must necessarily consider the human being as an appearance; then when we demand of them that they should also think of him qua intelligence as a thing in itself, they still persist in considering him in this respect too as an appearance. In this view it would no doubt be a contradiction to suppose the causality of the same subject (that is, his will) to be withdrawn from all the natural laws of the sensible world. But this contradiction disappears if they would only bethink themselves, and admit, as is reasonable, that behind the appearances there must also lie at their root (although hidden) the things in themselves, and that we cannot expect the laws of these to be the same as those that govern their appearances.

4.36.oldText: The subjective impossibility of explaining the freedom of the will is identical with the impossibility of discovering and explaining an interest * that a human being can take in the moral law. Nevertheless he does actually take an interest in it, the basis of which in us we call the moral feeling — which some have falsely assigned as the standard of our moral judgement, whereas it must rather be viewed as the subjective effect that the law exercises on the will, the objective principle of which is furnished by reason alone.

4.37.oldText: * Interest is that by which reason becomes practical — that is, a cause determining the will. Hence we say of rational beings only that they take an interest in a thing; irrational beings only feel sensual appetites. Reason takes a direct interest in action only when the universal validity of its maxims is alone sufficient to determine the will. Such an interest alone is pure. But if reason can determine the will only by means of another object of desire, or on the suggestion of a particular feeling of the subject, then it takes only an indirect interest in the action; and since reason by itself, without experience, cannot discover either objects of the will or a special feeling actuating it, this latter interest would only be empirical and not a pure rational interest. The logical interest of reason (namely, to extend its insight) is never direct, but presupposes purposes for which reason is employed.

4.38.oldText: For a rational being who is also affected through the senses to will what reason alone directs that such beings ought to will, it is no doubt required that reason should have the power to infuse a feeling of pleasure or satisfaction in the fulfilment of duty — that is, that it should have a causality by which it determines the sensibility according to its own principles. But it is quite impossible to discern, that is, to make intelligible a priori, how a mere thought, which itself contains nothing sensible, can itself produce a sensation of pleasure or pain. For this is a particular kind of causality, of which, as of every other causality, we can determine nothing whatever a priori; we must only consult experience about it. But since experience cannot supply us with any relation of cause and effect except between two objects of experience, whereas in this case, although indeed the effect produced lies within experience, the cause is supposed to be pure reason acting through mere ideas that offer no object to experience — it follows that for us human beings it is quite impossible to explain how and why the universality of the maxim as a law, that is, morality, interests us. This only is certain: it is not because it interests us that it has validity for us (for that would be heteronomy and dependence of practical reason on sensibility, namely, on a feeling as its principle, in which case it could never give moral laws); but rather it interests us because it is valid for us as human beings, inasmuch as it had its source in our will as intelligences — in other words, in our proper self — and what belongs to mere appearance is necessarily subordinated by reason to the nature of the thing in itself.

4.39.oldText: The question, then, "How is a categorical imperative possible?" can be answered to this extent, that we can assign the only hypothesis on which it is possible, namely, the idea of freedom; and we can also discern the necessity of this hypothesis. This is sufficient for the practical exercise of reason — that is, for the conviction of the validity of this imperative, and hence of the moral law. But how this hypothesis itself is possible can never be discerned by any human reason. On the hypothesis, however, that the will of an intelligence is free, its autonomy, as the essential formal condition of its determination, is a necessary consequence. Moreover, this freedom of will is not merely quite possible as a hypothesis (not involving any contradiction to the principle of physical necessity in the connection of the phenomena of the sensible world), as speculative philosophy can show; but further, a rational being who is conscious of causality through reason — that is to say, of a will (distinct from desires) — must of necessity make freedom practically (that is, in idea) the condition of all his voluntary actions. But to explain how pure reason can be of itself practical, without the aid of any spring of action that could be derived from any other source — that is, how the mere principle of the universal validity of all its maxims as laws (which would certainly be the form of a pure practical reason) can of itself supply a spring without any matter (object) of the will in which one could antecedently take any interest; and how it can produce an interest that would be called purely moral; or in other words, how pure reason can be practical — to explain this is beyond the power of human reason, and all the labour and pains of seeking an explanation of it are lost.

4.40.oldText: It is just the same as if I sought to find out how freedom itself is possible as the causality of a will. For then I quit the ground of philosophical explanation, and I have no other to go upon. I might indeed revel in the world of intelligences that still remains to me, but although I have an idea of it that is well founded, I have not the least knowledge of it, nor can I ever attain to such knowledge with all the efforts of my natural faculty of reason. It signifies only a something that remains over when I have eliminated everything belonging to the world of sense from the actuating principles of my will, serving merely to keep in bounds the principle of motives taken from the field of sensibility — fixing its limits and showing that it does not contain all in all within itself, but that there is more beyond it. But this something more I know no further. Of pure reason that frames this ideal, there remains, after the abstraction of all matter (that is, knowledge of objects), nothing but the form, namely, the practical law of the universality of the maxims, and, in conformity with this, the conception of reason in reference to a pure world of understanding as a possible efficient cause — that is, a cause determining the will. There must here be a total absence of springs, unless this idea of an intelligible world is itself the spring, or that in which reason primarily takes an interest; but to make this intelligible is precisely the problem we cannot solve.

4.41.oldText: Here now is the extreme limit of all moral inquiry, and it is of great importance to determine it, even for this reason, that reason may not on the one hand, to the prejudice of morals, seek about in the world of sense for the supreme motive and an interest comprehensible but empirical; and on the other hand, that it may not impotently flap its wings without being able to move in the (for it) empty space of transcendent concepts which we call the intelligible world, and so lose itself among chimeras. For the rest, the idea of a pure world of understanding as a system of all intelligences, to which we ourselves as rational beings belong (although we are likewise on the other side members of the sensible world), remains always a useful and legitimate idea for the purposes of rational belief, although all knowledge stops at its threshold — useful, namely, to produce in us a lively interest in the moral law by means of the noble ideal of a universal kingdom of ends in themselves (rational beings), to which we can belong as members only if we carefully conduct ourselves according to the maxims of freedom as if they were laws of nature.

4.43.oldText: The speculative employment of reason with respect to nature leads to the absolute necessity of some supreme cause of the world; the practical employment of reason with a view to freedom leads also to absolute necessity, but only of the laws of the actions of a rational being as such. Now it is an essential principle of reason, however employed, to push its knowledge to a consciousness of its necessity (without which it would not be rational knowledge). It is, however, an equally essential restriction of the same reason that it can neither discern the necessity of what is or what happens, nor of what ought to happen, unless a condition is supposed on which it is, happens, or ought to happen. In this way, however, by the constant inquiry for the condition, the satisfaction of reason is only further and further postponed. Hence it unceasingly seeks the unconditionally necessary and finds itself forced to assume it, although without any means of making it comprehensible to itself — happy enough if only it can discover a conception that agrees with this assumption. It is therefore no fault in our deduction of the supreme principle of morality, but an objection that should be made to human reason in general, that it cannot enable us to conceive the absolute necessity of an unconditional practical law (such as the categorical imperative must be). It cannot be blamed for refusing to explain this necessity by a condition — that is, by means of some interest assumed as a basis — since the law would then cease to be a supreme law of reason. And thus, while we do not comprehend the practical unconditional necessity of the moral imperative, we yet comprehend its incomprehensibility; and this is all that can be fairly demanded of a philosophy that strives to carry its principles up to the very limit of human reason.

1.0.oldText: Den antikke græske filosofi var inddelt i tre videnskaber: fysik, etik og logik. Denne inddeling passer perfekt til sagens natur. Den eneste forbedring, vi kan foretage, er at tilføje det princip, som inddelingen hviler på, så vi kan bekræfte dens fuldstændighed og identificere dens nødvendige underinddelinger korrekt.

1.1.oldText: Al fornuftsbaseret viden er enten materiel eller formel. Formel viden beskæftiger sig kun med forstandens og fornuftens form i sig selv — med tankens almene love, uanset hvad disse tanker handler om. Materiel viden beskæftiger sig med bestemte genstande og de love, der styrer dem. Formel filosofi kaldes logik. Materiel filosofi, som vedrører bestemte genstande og de love, de er underlagt, deler sig i to: lovene er enten naturlove eller frihedslove. Videnskaben om de første er fysik, videnskaben om de andre er etik. De kaldes også henholdsvis naturfilosofi og moralfilosofi.

1.2.oldText: Logikken kan ikke have nogen empirisk del — det vil sige ingen del, hvor tankens almene og nødvendige love skulle hvile på grunde hentet fra erfaringen. Ellers ville den slet ikke være logik, men kun en fejlbar optegnelse af, hvordan mennesker tilfældigvis tænker. En kanon for forstand og fornuft, gyldig for al tanke og påviselig, må være helt a priori. Naturfilosofi og moralfilosofi kan derimod hver have en empirisk del. Fysikken må bestemme naturens love som genstand for erfaringen; etikken må bestemme den menneskelige viljes love, for så vidt som den påvirkes af naturen. Fysikkens love beskriver, hvordan alting faktisk sker; etikkens love beskriver, hvordan alting bør ske. Etikken må også tage hensyn til de betingelser, hvorunder det, der bør ske, ofte ikke sker.

1.4.oldText: På denne måde opstår tanken om en dobbelt metafysik — en naturens metafysik og en moralens metafysik. Fysikken vil derfor have en empirisk del og en rationel del. Det samme gælder for etikken; men her kunne den empiriske del få det særlige navn praktisk antropologi, mens navnet moral er forbeholdt den rationelle del.

1.5.oldText: Alle erhverv, kunster og håndværk har haft gavn af arbejdsdelingen. I stedet for at én person gør alting, fokuserer hver på en bestemt slags arbejde, forskellig fra resten i de færdigheder, det kræver, så han kan gøre det lettere og til en højere standard. Hvor de forskellige slags arbejde ikke er adskilt, hvor enhver er altmuligmand, forbliver fremstillingen på det mest primitive niveau. Det kunne være værd at spørge, om ren filosofi i alle sine grene ikke kræver nogen, der er specifikt dedikeret til den. Ville hele videnskabens foretagende have gavn af, at de, der godt kan lide at blande det rationelle og det empiriske sammen i forhold ukendte selv for dem selv — folk, der for at behage publikums smag kalder sig selv uafhængige tænkere og afviser dem, der kun fokuserer på den rationelle del, som flueknepperier-filosoffer — blev advaret mod at forsøge at gøre to job på én gang, som kræver meget forskellige metoder, hver måske kræver sit eget særlige talent, og som forenet i én person kun frembringer fuskere? Men her spørger jeg kun, om videnskabens natur ikke kræver, at vi holder det empiriske og det rationelle strengt adskilt, og at vi sætter en naturens metafysik forud for den egentlige fysik (eller empirisk fysik), og en moralens metafysik forud for den praktiske antropologi. Moralens metafysik må renses for alt empirisk, så vi kan se, hvor meget den rene fornuft kan udrette i begge tilfælde, og fra hvilke kilder den henter sin a priori-lære. Denne undersøgelse må enten foretages af alle moralister (hvis navn er legion) eller af nogle, der føler et kald til den.

1.6.oldText: Eftersom min beskæftigelse her er moralfilosofi, indsnævrer jeg spørgsmålet til dette: er det ikke af største vigtighed at konstruere en ren moralfilosofi, som er fuldstændig renset for alt empirisk og hører under antropologien? At en sådan filosofi må være mulig, er indlysende ud fra den almene idé om pligt og moralloven. Enhver må indrømme, at hvis en lov skal have moralsk kraft — det vil sige være grundlaget for en forpligtelse — må den bære absolut nødvendighed med sig. Buddet »Du må ikke lyve« gælder for eksempel ikke alene for mennesker, som om andre fornuftsvæsener kunne ignorere det. Det samme gælder alle ægte morallove. Grundlaget for forpligtelsen må derfor ikke søges i menneskets natur eller i de omstændigheder i verden, hvor det befinder sig, men a priori i den rene fornufts begreb alene. Ethvert andet bud, der bygger på rene erfaringsprincipper, kan være alment i visse henseender; men i den udstrækning, det det allermindste hviler på empiriske grunde — selv blot for sit motiv — kan det være en praktisk regel, men aldrig en morallov.

1.7.oldText: Således er ikke alene morallovene og deres principper væsentligt adskilt fra enhver anden form for praktisk viden med noget empirisk i sig; al moralfilosofi hviler helt på sin rene del. Når den anvendes på et menneske, låner den intet som helst fra kundskaben om mennesket selv (antropologien), men giver det a priori-love som fornuftsvæsen. Disse love kræver ganske vist en dømmekraft skærpet af erfaring — først for at vide, i hvilke tilfælde de gælder, og dernæst for at få adgang til den menneskelige vilje og effektiv indflydelse på adfærd. Menneskene trækkes af så mange tilbøjeligheder, at de, selv om de er i stand til idéen om en praktisk ren fornuft, ikke så let kan gøre den virksom i deres liv.

1.8.oldText: En moralens metafysik er derfor uomgængeligt nødvendig — ikke blot af spekulative grunde, for at undersøge kilderne til de praktiske principper, der findes a priori i vor fornuft, men også fordi moralen selv er udsat for alle slags fordærvelse, så længe vi mangler den ledetråd og den øverste målestok, hvormed vi kan vurdere den korrekt. For at en handling skal være moralsk god, er det ikke nok, at den stemmer overens med moralloven; den må også gøres for lovens skyld. Ellers er overensstemmelsen kun tilfældig og usikker, eftersom et ikke-moralsk princip — selv om det undertiden kan frembringe handlinger, der stemmer overens med loven — også ofte vil frembringe handlinger, der modsiger den. Nu er det kun i en ren filosofi, vi kan søge moralloven i dens renhed og ægthed — og i en praktisk sag er dette af største vigtighed. Vi må derfor begynde med ren filosofi (metafysik), og uden den kan der ikke være nogen moralfilosofi overhovedet. Det, der blander rene principper med empiriske, fortjener ikke navnet filosofi; for det, der adskiller filosofien fra almen fornuftsbaseret viden, er, at filosofien behandler i adskilte videnskaber, hvad den almene viden kun fatter forvirret. Endnu mindre fortjener det navnet moralfilosofi, da det ved denne forvirring faktisk ødelægger moralens egen renhed og modarbejder sit eget formål.

1.9.oldText: Lad det ikke tænkes, at det, der her kræves, allerede findes i den propædeutik, som den berømte Wolf satte forud for sin moralfilosofi — nemlig hans såkaldte almene praktiske filosofi — og at vi derfor ikke har noget helt nyt felt at træde ind på. Netop fordi den var ment som en almen praktisk filosofi, overvejede den ikke nogen særlig art af vilje — sig en, der udelukkende var bestemt ud fra a priori-principper uden noget empirisk motiv, som vi kunne kalde en ren vilje. Den overvejede vilje i almindelighed, med alle de handlinger og betingelser, der falder under denne almene overskrift. Dette er, hvad der adskiller den fra en moralens metafysik, ligesom den almene logik, der behandler tankens almene akter og regler, adskiller sig fra den transcendentale filosofi, der behandler de særlige akter og regler for ren tanke — det vil sige tanke, hvis erkendelser er helt a priori. Moralens metafysik må undersøge idéen og principperne for en mulig ren vilje, ikke akterne og betingelserne for menneskelig vilje i almindelighed, der i vid udstrækning hentes fra psykologien. Det er sandt, at den almene moralfilosofi taler om morallove og pligt (i strid med al rimelighed). Men det er ingen indvending, for også her forbliver disse forfattere tro mod deres idé om emnet. De adskiller ikke de motiver, som fornuften alene foreskriver helt a priori — som er egentlig moralske — fra de empiriske motiver, som forstanden hæver til almene begreber blot ved sammenligning af erfaringer. Uden at lægge mærke til forskellen i deres kilder og behandle dem alle som ensartede, betragter de kun deres større eller mindre mængde. Sådan udformer de deres begreb om forpligtelse, som — selv om det er alt andet end moralsk — er alt, hvad der kan opnås i en filosofi, der slet ikke fælder dom om oprindelsen af alle mulige praktiske begreber — om de er a priori eller kun a posteriori.

1.10.oldText: Eftersom jeg har til hensigt at udgive en moralens metafysik senere, udsender jeg først disse Grundlæggende Principper. Der er egentlig intet andet fundament for en moralens metafysik end den kritiske undersøgelse af en ren praktisk fornuft — ligesom fundamentet for metafysikken er den kritiske undersøgelse af den rene spekulative fornuft, som allerede er udgivet. Men for det første er den kritiske undersøgelse af den rene praktiske fornuft ikke så absolut nødvendig som den af den spekulative fornuft, fordi den menneskelige fornuft i moralske spørgsmål let kan bringes til en høj grad af korrekthed og fuldstændighed, selv i den mest almindelige forstand, hvorimod den i sin teoretiske, men rene brug er helt dialektisk. For det andet, hvis kritikken af en ren praktisk fornuft skal være fuldstændig, må det også være muligt at vise dens identitet med den spekulative fornuft i et fælles princip, eftersom der i sidste ende kun kan være én og samme fornuft, adskilt blot i sin anvendelse. Jeg kunne dog ikke føre den til den fuldstændighed her uden at indføre overvejelser af en helt anden art, der kun ville forvirre læseren. Af denne grund har jeg kaldt dette værk Grundlæggende Principper for Moralens Metafysik snarere end En Kritisk Undersøgelse af den Rene Praktiske Fornuft.

1.11.oldText: For det tredje, eftersom en moralens metafysik — på trods af sin afskrækkende titel — er i stand til at fremstilles i populær form, tilpasset den almindelige forståelse, finder jeg det nyttigt at adskille denne foreløbige afhandling om dens grundlæggende principper fra den. På den måde behøver jeg ikke at trække disse uundgåeligt subtile diskussioner ind i en bog af mere enkel karakter.

1.12.oldText: Den foreliggende afhandling er intet andet end undersøgelsen og fastlæggelsen af moralens øverste princip. Dette alene udgør et studium, der er fuldstændigt i sig selv — et studium, der bør holdes adskilt fra enhver anden moralsk undersøgelse. Mine konklusioner i dette tunge spørgsmål, der hidtil er blevet meget utilfredsstillende behandlet, ville uden tvivl få betydelig støtte ved at anvende det samme princip på hele systemet, og ville blive stærkt bekræftet af den måde, hvorpå det ville vise sig tilstrækkeligt gennem det hele. Men jeg må give afkald på denne fordel, som trods alt ville være mere tilfredsstillende end nyttig. Et princips lette anvendelighed og dets tilsyneladende tilstrækkelighed giver intet virkelig sikkert bevis for dets soliditet; de har snarere tendens til at vække en partiskhed, der hindrer os i at undersøge og vurdere det strengt i sig selv, uden hensyn til konsekvenserne.

1.13.oldText: I dette arbejde har jeg valgt den metode, jeg finder mest passende, idet jeg går analytisk fra den almindelige viden til bestemmelsen af dens øverste princip, og dernæst stiger syntetisk ned fra undersøgelsen af dette princip og dets kilder tilbage til den almindelige viden, hvori vi finder det anvendt. Inddelingen bliver derfor som følger:

1.14.oldText: 1 FØRSTE AFSNIT. Overgang fra den almindelige fornuftsbaserede viden om moralen til den filosofiske.

1.15.oldText: 2 ANDET AFSNIT. Overgang fra populær moralfilosofi til moralens metafysik.

1.16.oldText: 3 TREDJE AFSNIT. Sidste skridt fra moralens metafysik til kritikken af den rene praktiske fornuft.

2.0.oldText: Intet i verden — eller endda uden for den — kan tænkes som godt uden forbehold, undtagen en god vilje. Intelligens, vid, dømmekraft og de øvrige åndelige talenter, hvad vi end kalder dem, eller mod, beslutsomhed, vedholdenhed, som temperamentskvaliteter, er utvivlsomt gode og ønskværdige på mange måder. Men disse naturens gaver kan også blive yderst dårlige og skadelige, hvis den vilje, der bruger dem — den vilje, der udgør, hvad vi kalder karakter — ikke er god. Det samme gælder lykkens gaver. Magt, rigdom, ære, selv sundhed, og den almene velvære og tilfredshed med ens vilkår, som vi kalder lykke, vækker stolthed og ofte hovmod, medmindre der er en god vilje til at rette deres indflydelse på sindet og derved hele handlingsprincippet og tilpasse det dets formål. Synet af et væsen, der ikke prydes af et eneste spor af en ren og god vilje, og som nyder ubrudt fremgang, kan aldrig give glæde til en upartisk fornuftig tilskuer. En god vilje synes da at være den uundværlige betingelse selv for at være lykken værdig.

2.1.oldText: Der er nogle egenskaber, som er nyttige for denne gode vilje selv og kan lette dens arbejde, men som ikke har nogen iboende ubetinget værdi, men altid forudsætter en god vilje, hvilket begrænser den agtelse, vi med rette har for dem, og forbyder os at betragte dem som absolut gode. Mådehold i affekter og lidenskaber, selvbeherskelse og rolig overvejelse er ikke blot gode på mange måder, men synes endda at være del af personens iboende værdi. Alligevel fortjener de langtfra at kaldes gode uden forbehold, selv om de gamle priste dem ubetinget. Uden den gode viljes principper kan de blive yderst dårlige: en skurks koldblodighed gør ham ikke blot langt farligere, men også direkte mere afskyelig i vore øjne, end han ville have været uden den.

2.2.oldText: En god vilje er god ikke på grund af, hvad den frembringer eller udretter, ikke på grund af dens egnethed til at nå et eller andet foreslået mål, men ganske enkelt i kraft af viljeshandlingen selv. Det vil sige, den er god i sig selv, og betragtet i sig selv skal den agtes langt højere end alt, hvad der kunne frembringes af den til fordel for nogen tilbøjelighed — eller endog summen af alle tilbøjeligheder. Selv om denne vilje ved en særlig ulykke eller ved en stedmoderlig naturs karrige forsyning skulle mangle al magt til at nå sit formål; selv om den med sine største anstrengelser intet skulle udrette, og der kun blev tilbage den gode vilje (ikke, naturligvis, et blot ønske, men opbydelsen af ethvert middel i vor magt) — så ville den, som en juvel, stadig skinne ved sit eget lys, som noget der har hele sin værdi i sig selv. Dens nyttighed eller frugtesløshed kan hverken lægge til eller trække fra denne værdi. Nyttighed ville være, så at sige, kun den indfatning, der lader os håndtere juvelen lettere i daglig handel, eller som tiltrækker opmærksomheden hos dem, der endnu ikke er kendere. Den kan ikke anbefale juvelen til sande kendere eller bestemme dens værdi.

2.3.oldText: Der er imidlertid noget så mærkeligt ved denne idé om den blotte viljes absolutte værdi — en idé, der slet ikke tager hensyn til nytte — at der trods selv den almindelige fornufts fulde tilslutning til den må opstå en mistanke om, at denne idé i virkeligheden måske er et produkt af blot højtsvævende fantasi, og at vi måske har misforstået naturens hensigt med at give fornuften som vor viljes styrer. Vi vil derfor undersøge denne idé fra det synspunkt.

2.4.oldText: I den fysiske konstitution af et organiseret væsen — det vil sige et væsen, der passende er tilpasset livets formål — antager vi som et grundlæggende princip, at intet organ til noget formål vil findes, undtagen det bedst egnede og tilpassede til det formål. Hvis nu naturens egentlige genstand i et væsen, der har fornuft og en vilje, var dets bevarelse, dets velfærd — kort sagt dets lykke — så havde naturen indrettet det meget dårligt ved at vælge skabningens fornuft til at udføre dette formål. Alle de handlinger, som skabningen skal udføre med dette formål for øje, og hele dens adfærdsregel, ville være langt sikrere foreskrevet for den af instinktet, og det mål ville være nået langt mere pålideligt, end fornuften nogensinde kunne opnå. Hvis fornuften var blevet givet til denne begunstigede skabning ud over instinktet, skulle den kun have tjent til at betragte hendes naturs lykkelige indretning, til at beundre den, til at lykønske sig selv med den og til at føle taknemmelighed for den over for den velgørende årsag — ikke til at underkaste hendes ønsker den svage og bedrageriske vejledning og fuskerisk at blande sig i naturens formål. Kort sagt ville naturen have sørget for, at fornuften ikke brød ud i praktisk udøvelse, og at den ikke med sin svage indsigt formastede sig til selv at udtænke lykkens plan og midlerne til at nå den. Naturen ville have påtaget sig valget ikke blot af målene, men også af midlerne, og med vis forudseenhed have betroet begge til instinktet.

2.5.oldText: Og faktisk finder vi, at jo mere en kultiveret fornuft med bevidst hensigt anvender sig på livets nydelse og lykke, jo mere falder personen ud af sand tilfredsstillelse. Heraf opstår hos mange — hvis de er ærlige nok til at indrømme det — en vis grad af misologi, det vil sige had til fornuften, især hos dem, der er mest erfarne i dens brug. Efter at have beregnet alle de fordele, de udleder — jeg vil ikke sige fra opfindelsen af alle de almindelige luksuriøse kunster, men selv fra videnskaberne (som synes dem trods alt kun at være en luksus for forstanden) — finder de, at de faktisk kun har bragt mere bekymring på deres skuldre snarere end vundet i lykke. De ender med at misunde snarere end foragte den mere almindelige slags mennesker, der holder sig tættere til det blotte instinkts vejledning og ikke lader fornuften få megen indflydelse på deres adfærd. Vi må indrømme, at dommen hos dem, der meget gerne ville sænke den ophøjede lovprisning af de fordele, fornuften giver os med hensyn til livets lykke og tilfredshed, eller som endda ville reducere dem under nul, på ingen måde er sur eller utaknemmelig over for den godhed, hvormed verden styres. Til grund for disse domme ligger idéen om, at vor eksistens har et anderledes og langt ædlere mål, til hvilket — og ikke til lykken — fornuften egentlig er bestemt, og som derfor må betragtes som den øverste betingelse, til hvilken menneskenes private mål for det meste må underordnes.

2.6.oldText: For fornuften er ikke kompetent til med sikkerhed at vejlede viljen vedrørende dens genstande og tilfredsstillelsen af alle vore behov (som den endda i nogen grad mangedobler); et indplantet instinkt ville have ført til det mål med langt større sikkerhed. Alligevel er fornuften os givet som en praktisk evne — det vil sige, som en, der skal have indflydelse på viljen. Hvis man indrømmer, at naturen i fordelingen af sine evner har tilpasset midler til formål, må fornuftens sande bestemmelse være at frembringe en vilje, der ikke blot er god som middel til noget andet, men god i sig selv. Til dette var fornuften absolut nødvendig. Denne vilje må, selv om den ikke er det eneste og fuldstændige gode, være det øverste gode og betingelsen for ethvert andet, selv for ønsket om lykke. Under disse omstændigheder er der intet i strid med naturens visdom i den kendsgerning, at dyrkelsen af fornuften, som kræves til det første og ubetingede formål, på mange måder griber ind — i hvert fald i dette liv — i opnåelsen af det andet, som altid er betinget, nemlig lykken. Den kan endda reducere lykken til intet, uden at naturen derved svigter sit formål. For fornuften anerkender etableringen af en god vilje som sin højeste praktiske bestemmelse, og er i opnåelsen af dette formål kun i stand til en tilfredsstillelse af sin egen art — nemlig den, der kommer af at nå et mål bestemt af fornuften alene, selv om dette kan medføre mange skuffelser for tilbøjelighedernes mål.

2.7.oldText: Vi må nu udvikle begrebet om en vilje, der fortjener at agtes højt for sin egen skyld og er god uden hensyn til noget videre — et begreb, der allerede findes i sund naturlig forstand, snarere har brug for at blive klargjort end at blive undervist, og som ved vurderingen af vore handlingers værdi altid tager førstepladsen og udgør betingelsen for alle de øvrige. For at gøre dette vil vi tage begrebet pligt, som omfatter en god vilje, om end under visse subjektive begrænsninger og hindringer. Disse skjuler dog langtfra den gode vilje eller gør den ukendelig, men bringer den snarere frem ved kontrast og får den til at skinne så meget desto klarere.

2.8.oldText: Jeg lader her alle handlinger ude af betragtning, som allerede er anerkendt som uforenelige med pligten, selv om de kan være nyttige til dette eller hint formål. For ved disse kan spørgsmålet om, hvorvidt de gøres af pligt, slet ikke opstå, da de faktisk strider mod pligten. Jeg lægger også til side de handlinger, der virkelig stemmer overens med pligten, men som folk ikke har nogen direkte tilbøjelighed til at udføre, og som de kun gør, fordi de drives dertil af en anden tilbøjelighed. For i dette tilfælde er det let at se, om handlingen, der stemmer overens med pligten, gøres af pligt eller af et selvisk motiv. Det er langt sværere at gøre denne skelnen, når handlingen stemmer overens med pligten, og subjektet også har en direkte tilbøjelighed til den. For eksempel er det altid en handelsmands pligt ikke at overpris-tage en uerfaren kunde; og overalt, hvor der er megen handel, overpris-tager den kloge købmand ikke, men holder en fast pris for alle, så et barn kan købe hos ham lige så godt som enhver anden. Folk bliver således ærligt betjent. Men det er ikke nok til at få os til at tro, at købmanden har handlet af pligt og ud fra ærlighedsprincipper: hans egen fordel krævede det. Det er udelukket i dette tilfælde at antage, at han desuden kunne have en direkte tilbøjelighed til fordel for sine kunder, så han ud af kærlighed ikke skulle give nogen en fordel frem for en anden. Følgelig blev handlingen hverken gjort af pligt eller af direkte tilbøjelighed, men kun af et selvisk motiv.

2.9.oldText: På den anden side er det en pligt at bevare sit liv, og desuden har alle en direkte tilbøjelighed til at gøre det. Men derfor har den ofte ængstelige omsorg, de fleste mennesker har for deres liv, ingen iboende værdi, og deres maksime har ingen moralsk betydning. De bevarer deres liv, som pligten kræver, det er sikkert, men ikke fordi pligten kræver det. På den anden side, hvis modgang og håbløs sorg fuldstændigt har slået smagen for livet ihjel; hvis den uheldige, stærk i sind, harmfuld over sin skæbne snarere end fortvivlet eller modløs, ønsker døden, og dog bevarer sit liv uden at elske det — ikke af tilbøjelighed eller frygt, men af pligt — så har hans maksime moralsk værdi.

2.10.oldText: Det er en pligt at være venlig mod andre, når vi kan. Ud over dette er der mange mennesker så sympatisk indrettede, at de uden noget motiv af forfængelighed eller egennytte finder fornøjelse i at sprede glæde omkring sig og kan glæde sig over andres tilfredshed, når den er deres eget værk. Men jeg fastholder, at i et sådant tilfælde har en handling af denne art, hvor passende og elskværdig den end måtte være, alligevel ingen sand moralsk værdi. Den er på linje med andre tilbøjeligheder — for eksempel tilbøjeligheden til ære, som, hvis den tilfældigvis er rettet mod, hvad der i virkeligheden er af offentlig nytte og i overensstemmelse med pligten og derfor ærefuld, fortjener ros og opmuntring, men ikke agtelse. Maksimen mangler den moralske betydning — nemlig, at sådanne handlinger gøres af pligt, ikke af tilbøjelighed. Antag, at filantropens sind blev formørket af hans egen sorg, der udslukkede al sympati for andres lod, og at han, mens han stadig har magt til at hjælpe andre i nød, ikke berøres af deres bekymring, fordi han er optaget af sin egen. Antag nu, at han river sig løs af denne døde ufølsomhed og udfører handlingen uden nogen tilbøjelighed til den, men ganske enkelt af pligt — så har hans handling for første gang sin ægte moralske værdi. Endnu mere: hvis naturen har lagt lidt sympati i dette eller hint menneskes hjerte; hvis han, et retskaffent menneske efter hypotesen, af temperament er kold og ligegyldig over for andres lidelser, måske fordi han med hensyn til sine egne er udstyret med den særlige gave tålmodighed og udholdenhed, og antager — eller endda kræver — at andre skulle have det samme; og en sådan person ville bestemt ikke være naturens laveste produkt — men hvis naturen ikke havde gjort ham særligt egnet til at være filantrop, ville han da ikke stadig finde i sig selv en kilde, hvorfra han kunne give sig selv en langt højere værdi end den, et godmodigt temperament kunne give? Utvivlsomt. Det er netop heri, at karakterens moralske værdi bringes frem, hvilket er ulige det højeste af alt: at han er venlig, ikke af tilbøjelighed, men af pligt.

2.11.oldText: At sikre sin egen lykke er en pligt, i det mindste indirekte; for utilfredshed med sin tilstand, under presset af mange bekymringer og midt i utilfredsstillede behov, kunne let blive en stor fristelse til at krænke pligten. Men også her, uden at se på pligten, har alle mennesker allerede den stærkeste og mest intime tilbøjelighed til lykke, fordi det netop er i denne idé, at alle tilbøjeligheder forenes til én helhed. Lykkens bud er imidlertid ofte af en sådan art, at det i høj grad griber ind i nogle tilbøjeligheder, og dog kan en person ikke danne sig nogen bestemt og sikker forestilling om summen af tilfredsstillelsen af dem alle, som kaldes lykke.
